undermine

/un-der-MYN/ — stress on the last syllable · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To undermine something is to weaken it little by little by eating away at its support or foundation.

Rumors undermined the manager's authority long before the vote.

Example

For weeks, the rival candidate released stories suggesting the mayor had mismanaged funds, each one undermining her credibility with voters a little more.

The weakening here is deliberate and gradual — each story chipped away at her standing, not all at once but little by little from beneath. Undermine is more precise than 'damage' because it captures that slow, hidden weakening of support from underneath, like digging away at a foundation.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sabotage: Sabotage means to wreck something on purpose, and it needs a person acting on purpose - a saboteur cutting wires or spoiling plans, often in one destructive stroke. Undermine is slower and quieter: it eats away at something's support little by little until it gives way.

subvert: Subvert aims at an authority or a system - a government, a set of rules - and means secretly working to overturn it from within. Undermine is wider: you can undermine a friend's confidence or an argument, gradually wearing away whatever holds it up.

destabilize: Destabilize means to make something shaky and likely to fall, and it describes the wobbling result - a destabilized market, a destabilized ladder. Undermine points at the method instead: quietly digging away at the support underneath, which is one particular way of making something unsteady.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

bolster: to prop up and strengthen something's support

support: to hold something up and help it stand

Where it sits · how destructive the action becomes

doubt → weaken → demolish → undermine

doubt vs. undermine: Doubt is only a seed compared with undermine: to doubt a leader is to question her privately, while to undermine her is to quietly chip away at her actual support.

weaken vs. undermine: Weaken is broader and often milder than undermine; anything can weaken something openly, but to undermine is to weaken it from underneath — secretly, at its foundation.

demolish vs. undermine: Demolish is the most violent of the four — it flattens something in one blow — while undermine works slowly and invisibly, removing support piece by piece until things collapse.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — under-: beneath, below (Old English)

Root — mine: to dig (Old French)

Put it together: Under- means 'beneath' and mine means 'to dig' — undermining was originally a siege tactic of digging tunnels beneath a castle wall so it would collapse. Today it means weakening anything by quietly attacking its foundation.

Use the root in a new word: miner: The retired miner still keeps his old headlamp and boots on a hook by the back door.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Undermine is the word when something is being weakened from the inside or from its foundation, often secretly or gradually. Use it for authority, credibility, trust, or arguments being slowly eroded. For straightforward damage or direct attack, simpler words like 'weaken' or 'damage' are better choices.
